title: The water cycle
summary: Follow a drop of water as it rises into the sky, makes a cloud, falls as rain, and starts all over again.
objective: Name the four steps of the water cycle and spot each one in everyday life.

hook.prompt: After the rain, there's a puddle on the sidewalk. By the afternoon, the sun is out and the puddle is gone. Where did the water go?

options.text: Up into the air
Down into the sidewalk
options.feedback: A sidewalk is hard, so the water can't sink in. It went somewhere else!

options.text: The sun burned it up
options.feedback: Water can't burn. It changed into something you can't see.

hook.explanation: The water floated up into the air, even though nobody saw it go. Let's find out how.

bricks.title: The sun lifts water into the air
bricks.body: When the sun warms water, some of it turns into a gas called **water vapor**. You can't see it, but it floats up into the air. This change is called **evaporation**. Water doesn't need to boil to evaporate. That's why wet swimsuits dry on a sunny day. The warmer it is, the faster water evaporates.

term.definition: When liquid water turns into invisible water vapor and rises into the air.

bricks.prompt: Two wet towels hang outside. One is in the sun, and one is in the shade. Which one dries first?

options.text: The towel in the sun
The towel in the shade
options.feedback: The shade keeps the towel cooler, so its water evaporates more slowly.

options.text: They dry at the same time
options.feedback: Warmth speeds up evaporation, so one towel has a big head start.

bricks.hint: Does warmth make evaporation faster or slower?
bricks.explanation: The sun warms the towel, and warmer water evaporates faster. So the sunny towel dries first.

bricks.prompt: A glass of water sits on a windowsill for a week. Nobody drinks from it, but the water gets lower and lower. Where did the missing water go?

options.text: It evaporated into the air as water vapor
It soaked into the glass
options.feedback: Glass isn't like a sponge. It can't soak up water.

options.text: Nowhere: water can only leave a glass if it boils
options.feedback: Water doesn't need to boil to evaporate. It slowly turns into vapor even at room temperature.

bricks.hint: Remember the wet swimsuit drying in the sun.
bricks.explanation: A little water evaporates every day, even without boiling. Over a week, that adds up to a lower water level.

bricks.title: Cold air turns vapor into clouds
bricks.body: Water vapor rises high into the sky, where the air is **cold**. The cold turns the vapor back into tiny drops of liquid water. This is called **condensation**. Billions of tiny drops together make a **cloud**. You can see condensation at home too. Drops appear on the outside of a cold glass of juice, because the vapor in the air touches the cold glass and turns back into water.

term.definition: When water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water.

visual.alt: Dashed arrows of water vapor rise from the warm ground to the cold air up high, where a gray cloud is full of tiny blue drops.

bricks.prompt: You take a cold can of lemonade out of the fridge. Soon the outside of the can is covered in little drops. Where did the drops come from?

options.text: Water vapor in the air touched the cold can and turned into drops
Lemonade leaked out through the can
options.feedback: The can is closed tight, and the drops are plain water, not lemonade.

options.text: The can is sweating, like you do after running
options.feedback: Cans can't sweat. The water came from the air around the can.

bricks.hint: What happens to water vapor when it touches something cold?
bricks.explanation: The cold can cools the vapor in the air next to it, and the vapor condenses into drops, just like on the cold glass of juice.

bricks.prompt: Water vapor rises from the ground. High up in the sky, it turns into a cloud. What makes that happen?

options.text: The air up high is cold
The air up high is hot, because it's closer to the sun
options.feedback: It's actually colder up high. And it's cold, not heat, that turns vapor back into drops.

options.text: The wind squashes the vapor together
options.feedback: Wind pushes clouds around, but it doesn't make them. Cold air does.

bricks.hint: Is it cold or warm that turns vapor back into water?
bricks.explanation: High in the sky the air is cold. The cold turns the vapor into tiny drops, and lots of tiny drops make a cloud.

bricks.prompt: Is water turning into vapor, or vapor turning into drops? Sort each one.

items.text: Wet hair drying in the sun
A puddle shrinking on a hot day
Drops on a cold glass of milk
A bathroom mirror getting foggy after a hot shower
Your breath making a cold car window foggy

bricks.hint: Is water leaving something, or are drops showing up on something cold?
bricks.explanation: When things dry, water evaporates away. When drops or fog appear on something cold, vapor is condensing onto it.

bricks.title: Rain falls, and it all starts again
bricks.body: Inside a cloud, tiny drops bump together and grow. When they get too heavy to float, they fall. Water falling from clouds is called **precipitation**. It can be rain, or snow and hail when it's cold enough to freeze. The water **collects** in rivers, lakes, oceans, and the ground. Then the sun warms it, and it evaporates again. Round and round it goes!

term.definition: The never-ending trip water takes: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection, again and again.

options.text: Rain
Snow
Hail
A cloud floating by
options.feedback: A cloud's drops are still floating. Precipitation is water falling from the cloud.

options.text: Drops on a cold window
options.feedback: Those drops came out of the air onto something cold. That's condensation.

bricks.hint: Precipitation is water that falls from a cloud.
bricks.explanation: Rain, snow, and hail all fall from clouds, so they're all precipitation. Snow and hail are just frozen water.

bricks.prompt: A big rainstorm fills up a lake. What happens to that lake water next in the water cycle?

options.text: The sun warms it, and some of it evaporates into the air again
It stays in the lake forever
options.feedback: The sun keeps warming the lake, so some water keeps rising as vapor. That's why it's a cycle.

options.text: It floats straight back up to the cloud as raindrops
options.feedback: Raindrops can't float up. Water only rises after it evaporates into invisible vapor.

bricks.hint: The water cycle goes round and round. What step comes after collection?
bricks.explanation: After water collects in a lake, the sun warms it and it evaporates. Then the whole cycle starts again.

challenge.prompt: You tape a closed plastic bag with a little water in it to a sunny window. Put what happens inside the bag in order.

visual.html: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 170' class='w-full max-w-sm' direction='ltr'><rect x='10' y='10' width='220' height='150' rx='6' fill='none' class='stroke-border' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='200' cy='38' r='14' class='fill-amber-400'/><rect x='70' y='30' width='90' height='115' rx='10' fill='none' class='stroke-muted-foreground' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='70' y1='42' x2='160' y2='42' class='stroke-muted-foreground' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M71 112 L159 112 L159 135 Q159 144 150 144 L80 144 Q71 144 71 135 Z' class='fill-sky-500'/><rect x='95' y='22' width='40' height='12' rx='2' class='fill-amber-200'/></svg>
visual.alt: A closed plastic bag taped to a window, with a little blue water at the bottom and the sun shining outside.

items.text: The sun warms the water at the bottom of the bag
Invisible vapor rises up inside the bag
Tiny drops appear near the top of the bag
The drops join together and slide down
The water gathers at the bottom again

challenge.hint: Start with what the sun does, and follow the water all the way round.
challenge.explanation: It's a tiny water cycle: the water evaporates, condenses into drops, falls back down, and collects at the bottom. Then it starts again.

takeaways: The sun warms water and turns it into invisible vapor that rises. That's evaporation.
Up high, cold air turns vapor back into tiny drops that make clouds. That's condensation.
Heavy drops fall as rain, snow, or hail, collect in lakes and oceans, and then the cycle starts again.
